title: C - Test 1: Core Fundamentals & Patterns
description: Comprehensive technical evaluation for C covering runtime mechanics, design principles, and problem solving.

questions.question: [C • Test 1 • Q1] Which bitwise operation toggles the k-th bit of an integer variable 'num' without altering other bits?
options: num = num >> k
num ^= (1 << k) (XOR with a single-bit mask).
questions.correctAnswer: num ^= (1 << k) (XOR with a single-bit mask).
questions.explanation: Bitwise XOR with 1 flips the bit (0->1, 1->0), while XOR with 0 preserves original bit state.
questions.hint: XOR with 1 toggles; OR sets; AND with NOT clears.
questions.relatedConcept: C - Bitwise Operators & Masking
questions.interviewTip: Bit manipulation is evaluated in all embedded, firmware, and low-level screening rounds.

questions.question: [C • Test 1 • Q2] What determines the memory alignment padding inserted by modern C compilers inside structs?
options: Always strictly packs bytes with zero gaps.
Aligns member offsets to multiples of member size (e.g. 8-byte boundary for double), padding struct to a multiple of largest member.
Aligns all variables to 64-byte cache line boundaries.
Padding depends only on operating system file system block size.
questions.correctAnswer: Aligns member offsets to multiples of member size (e.g. 8-byte boundary for double), padding struct to a multiple of largest member.
questions.explanation: CPUs read words faster when aligned to natural boundaries. The double member (8 bytes) requires 8-byte offset alignment.
questions.hint: Largest member alignment constraint dictates total struct sizing.
questions.relatedConcept: C - Struct Alignment & Padding
questions.interviewTip: Arrange struct members from largest to smallest to minimize padding waste.

questions.question: [C • Test 1 • Q3] Why does executing '*ptr = 'Z';' on 'char *ptr = "Data";' crash with Segmentation Fault on Unix/Linux?
options: Heap memory was exhausted.
Pointer was null.
Pointers to char can only hold ASCII 0-127.
String literals are placed in read-only text (.rodata) memory segment by the linker.
questions.correctAnswer: String literals are placed in read-only text (.rodata) memory segment by the linker.
questions.explanation: Modifying write-protected memory pages causes the CPU memory management unit (MMU) to trigger a segmentation violation.
questions.hint: String literals live in read-only text segments.
questions.relatedConcept: C - String Literal Immutability
questions.interviewTip: Use 'char str[] = "Data";' to allocate mutable stack storage.

questions.question: [C • Test 1 • Q4] When evaluating pointer expression '*(arr + 3)' where 'int arr[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};', what value is retrieved?
options: 30 (dereferences index 2).
40 (dereferences index 3 directly).
Address of arr[3].
Garbage memory value.
questions.correctAnswer: 40 (dereferences index 3 directly).
questions.explanation: *(arr + i) is mathematically identical to arr[i]. With offset 3, it fetches the 4th element (40).
questions.hint: arr[i] is defined as *(arr + i) in standard C.
questions.relatedConcept: C - Pointer Arithmetic & Array Strides
questions.interviewTip: Pointer subscript symmetry means 3[arr] is also valid C syntax!

questions.question: [C • Test 1 • Q5] What occurs if a function returns a pointer to a local stack array 'int local[10]' in C?
options: Stack frame is automatically preserved in heap.
Triggers a mandatory compiler abort.
Memory is promoted to static global scope.
Returns a dangling pointer to deallocated stack memory, causing undefined behavior on access.
questions.correctAnswer: Returns a dangling pointer to deallocated stack memory, causing undefined behavior on access.
questions.explanation: Stack frames are invalidated upon function return. Accessing returned stack pointers invokes undefined behavior.
questions.hint: Stack allocations are freed when function returns.
questions.relatedConcept: C - Dynamic Heap vs Stack Lifetime
questions.interviewTip: Always use malloc() or pass a buffer pointer from caller if data must outlive function execution.

title: C++ - Test 1: Core Fundamentals & Patterns
description: Comprehensive technical evaluation for C++ covering runtime mechanics, design principles, and problem solving.

questions.question: [C++ • Test 1 • Q1] What distinguishes 'std::unique_ptr' from 'std::shared_ptr' regarding memory and copy semantics?
options: std::unique_ptr uses garbage collection, shared_ptr does not.
std::unique_ptr is strictly non-copyable with single exclusive ownership; std::shared_ptr uses reference counting on a shared control block.
std::unique_ptr cannot be placed in STL containers.
Both have identical copy constructors.
questions.correctAnswer: std::unique_ptr is strictly non-copyable with single exclusive ownership; std::shared_ptr uses reference counting on a shared control block.
questions.explanation: unique_ptr has zero memory overhead (same size as raw pointer). shared_ptr allocates an atomic control block for reference count tracking.
questions.hint: Move-only exclusive ownership vs reference-counted shared ownership.
questions.relatedConcept: C++ - RAII & Smart Pointer Ownership
questions.interviewTip: Prefer std::make_unique and std::make_shared over raw new allocations.

questions.question: [C++ • Test 1 • Q2] In modern C++11+, what is the fundamental purpose of 'std::move()'?
options: Moves execution to a parallel background thread.
Frees the memory of variable 'a' immediately.
Clones vector 'a' on stack memory.
Unconditionally casts an lvalue to an rvalue reference (&&) to enable ownership transfer without deep copy.
questions.correctAnswer: Unconditionally casts an lvalue to an rvalue reference (&&) to enable ownership transfer without deep copy.
questions.explanation: std::move does not move anything at runtime; it performs a static_cast to rvalue reference so the move constructor steals internal pointers.
questions.hint: Cast to rvalue reference enabling pointer pilfering.
questions.relatedConcept: C++ - Move Semantics & Rvalue References
questions.interviewTip: Remember that moved-from objects remain in a valid but unspecified state.

questions.question: [C++ • Test 1 • Q3] How does dynamic polymorphism achieve runtime function dispatch in C++?
options: By re-compiling bytecode on demand.
Through a hidden vptr pointer in the object pointing to the class vtable (array of virtual function pointers).
Through runtime hash table lookup by method name.
Using reflection metadata loaded in Heap.
questions.correctAnswer: Through a hidden vptr pointer in the object pointing to the class vtable (array of virtual function pointers).
questions.explanation: Each polymorphic class generates a vtable. Object instantiation initializes vptr to point to the appropriate class vtable.
questions.hint: vptr inside object points to vtable array of function addresses.
questions.relatedConcept: C++ - Virtual Table & Dynamic Dispatch
questions.interviewTip: Virtual calls incur a slight pointer indirection cost and prevent some inlining optimizations.

title: Java - Test 1: Core Fundamentals & Patterns
description: Comprehensive technical evaluation for Java covering runtime mechanics, design principles, and problem solving.

questions.question: [Java • Test 1 • Q1] What does the 'volatile' keyword guarantee in Java multithreading?
options: Provides complete synchronized locking on the variable.
Prevents the object from being garbage collected.
Guarantees memory visibility across threads by reading/writing directly to main memory, without providing mutual exclusion/atomicity.
Makes compound operations like count++ atomic.
questions.correctAnswer: Guarantees memory visibility across threads by reading/writing directly to main memory, without providing mutual exclusion/atomicity.
questions.explanation: Volatile prevents CPU caching and instruction reordering for that variable, ensuring changes by one thread are immediately visible to all others.
questions.hint: Visibility guarantee, not atomic locking.
questions.relatedConcept: Java - Volatile vs Synchronized
questions.interviewTip: For compound atomic operations, use AtomicInteger / AtomicReference instead of volatile.

questions.question: [Java • Test 1 • Q2] What will be printed by 'System.out.println(s1 == s2);' when 'String s1 = "Java"; String s2 = new String("Java");'?
options: false (s1 references String Constant Pool, s2 references a distinct Heap object).
true (JVM string deduplication merges references).
Compilation Error.
NullPointerException.
questions.correctAnswer: false (s1 references String Constant Pool, s2 references a distinct Heap object).
questions.explanation: == compares object memory addresses. Literal references the String Pool; 'new String()' allocates a separate Heap instance.
questions.hint: Use .equals() for content comparison, == compares references.
questions.relatedConcept: Java - String Pool & Immutability
questions.interviewTip: Calling s2.intern() returns the pooled canonical reference.

questions.question: [Java • Test 1 • Q3] In Java 8+, what happens when a HashMap bucket collision list reaches 8 elements (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD)?
options: Throws a MaxBucketCollisionException.
Rehashes all keys into a flat array.
The linked list bucket converts into a balanced Red-Black Tree (TreeNode), reducing lookup time to O(log n).
Discards oldest entries via LRU policy.
questions.correctAnswer: The linked list bucket converts into a balanced Red-Black Tree (TreeNode), reducing lookup time to O(log n).
questions.explanation: Java 8 converts linked lists (O(n) worst case) to Red-Black self-balancing trees (O(log n) worst case) once table capacity >= 64 and bucket >= 8.
questions.hint: Linked list treeifies into Red-Black Tree.
questions.relatedConcept: Java - HashMap Internal Architecture
questions.interviewTip: Ensure custom keys implement consistent equals() and hashCode() methods.

questions.question: [Java • Test 1 • Q9] In Java 8+, what happens when a HashMap bucket collision list reaches 8 elements (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD)?
options: Throws a MaxBucketCollisionException.

The linked list bucket converts into a balanced Red-Black Tree (TreeNode), reducing lookup time to O(log n).

questions.relatedConcept: Java - HashMap Internal Architecture
questions.interviewTip: Ensure custom keys implement consistent equals() and hashCode() methods.

questions.relatedConcept: Java - Volatile vs Synchronized
questions.interviewTip: For compound atomic operations, use AtomicInteger / AtomicReference instead of volatile.

questions.question: [Python • Test 1 • Q1] What is the primary advantage of using a generator expression '(x*2 for x in data)' over list comprehension '[x*2 for x in data]'?
options: Generators evaluate lazily on-demand using O(1) memory, avoiding allocating the full list in RAM.
Generators execute 100x faster on GPU.
List comprehensions cannot be iterated in for loops.
Generators automatically save output to disk.
questions.correctAnswer: Generators evaluate lazily on-demand using O(1) memory, avoiding allocating the full list in RAM.
questions.explanation: Generators yield items one at a time using iterator protocol, making them essential for processing gigabyte-scale datasets.
questions.hint: Lazy evaluation saves RAM.
questions.relatedConcept: Python - Generator Memory Efficiency
questions.interviewTip: Generators are ideal for streaming log files or continuous database cursor streams.

questions.question: [Python • Test 1 • Q2] What is the output of calling 'def fn(val, acc=[]): acc.append(val); return acc' twice with fn(1) then fn(2)?
questions.codeSnippet:
def fn(val, acc=[]):
    acc.append(val)
    return acc
print(fn(1))
print(fn(2))
options: [1] then [2]
[1] then [1, 2] (default list object is bound ONCE at function definition time).
TypeError: default argument modified
questions.correctAnswer: [1] then [1, 2] (default list object is bound ONCE at function definition time).
questions.explanation: Default parameter values are evaluated once when def executes. The same list object is shared across subsequent invocations.
questions.hint: Use 'acc=None' inside function signature to create fresh default lists.
questions.relatedConcept: Python - Mutable Default Arguments
questions.interviewTip: Always use None as default value for mutable arguments in Python.

questions.question: [Python • Test 1 • Q3] How does the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) impact multithreading in CPython?
options: Restricts execution of Python bytecode to a single native thread at a time, limiting CPU-bound speedup across multiple cores.
Prevents memory leaks during asyncio coroutines.
Enforces static types on all global variables.
Bans socket networking over multiple threads.
questions.correctAnswer: Restricts execution of Python bytecode to a single native thread at a time, limiting CPU-bound speedup across multiple cores.
questions.explanation: GIL protects CPython memory management. CPU-bound code requires multiprocessing to achieve true multi-core parallelism.
questions.hint: One thread executes bytecode at a time in CPython.
questions.relatedConcept: Python - GIL & Concurrency Boundaries
questions.interviewTip: Use multiprocessing for CPU heavy tasks, threading/asyncio for I/O bound tasks.

Every class must inherit from exactly one parent.
Classes should be open for modification and closed for extension.
Dependencies must be hardcoded statically.
questions.correctAnswer: Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without altering program correctness.
questions.explanation: LSP guarantees that derived classes honor the contract and behavior expectations established by the base type.
questions.hint: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types.
questions.relatedConcept: TCS - Object Oriented Design & SOLID Principles
questions.interviewTip: Violating LSP often occurs when overriding methods with empty implementations or unexpected exceptions.

questions.question: [TCS • Test 1 • Q6] In Distributed Storage, how does Consistent Hashing minimize partition migration when a node is added?
options: Rehashes all keys across all servers from scratch.
Duplicates all partitions to every machine in cluster.
Maps servers and keys to a 360-degree hash ring, so adding a node only migrates k/N keys from its immediate neighbor.
Freezes all transactions until rebalancing completes.
questions.correctAnswer: Maps servers and keys to a 360-degree hash ring, so adding a node only migrates k/N keys from its immediate neighbor.
questions.explanation: Consistent Hashing ensures that only adjacent ring segments are redistributed, minimizing network transfer during cluster scaling.
questions.hint: Hash ring bounds key migration to immediate neighbors.
questions.relatedConcept: TCS - Consistent Hashing in Distributed Systems
questions.interviewTip: Amazon DynamoDB and Cassandra use consistent hashing with virtual nodes.

questions.question: [TCS • Test 1 • Q7] Which SQL transaction isolation level prevents Dirty Reads and Non-Repeatable Reads, but may allow Phantom Reads?
options: REPEATABLE READ
READ COMMITTED
READ UNCOMMITTED
SERIALIZABLE
questions.correctAnswer: REPEATABLE READ
questions.explanation: Repeatable Read locks scanned rows preventing updates, but standard SQL allows concurrent transactions to insert new matching rows (phantoms).
questions.hint: Read Uncommitted < Read Committed < Repeatable Read < Serializable.
questions.relatedConcept: TCS - ACID Isolation & Concurrency Anomalies
questions.interviewTip: Serializable eliminates all anomalies via strict range locking or SSI.

questions.question: [TCS • Test 1 • Q8] Why do database storage engines (InnoDB, Postgres) utilize B+ Trees instead of standard Binary Search Trees?
options: B+ Trees eliminate all disk writes.
Binary trees cannot store string keys.
High fan-out minimizes disk I/O depth (O(log_B N)), and linked leaf nodes allow sequential range scans.
B+ Trees automatically compress data in RAM.
questions.correctAnswer: High fan-out minimizes disk I/O depth (O(log_B N)), and linked leaf nodes allow sequential range scans.
questions.explanation: B+ Trees store records only in linked leaves. The wide branching factor (high fan-out) reduces tree height to 3-4 levels for millions of rows.
questions.hint: High fan-out reduces disk page reads.
questions.relatedConcept: TCS - B+ Tree Indexing & Range Lookups
questions.interviewTip: Understand covering index (index-only scan) optimization for SQL queries.

questions.question: [TCS • Test 1 • Q9] What is the primary purpose of the Circuit Breaker pattern in microservice architecture?
options: Fails fast when downstream services become unresponsive, preventing cascading thread starvation across the system.
Encrypts payload traffic with TLS.
Balances network load across all containers.
Compresses JSON responses.
questions.correctAnswer: Fails fast when downstream services become unresponsive, preventing cascading thread starvation across the system.
questions.explanation: Circuit Breakers track failure rates and trip Open to reject requests immediately, returning fallback responses until health recovers.
questions.hint: Fails fast to protect system resilience.
questions.relatedConcept: TCS - Microservices Circuit Breaker Pattern
questions.interviewTip: Always define fallbacks and reasonable timeout thresholds for HTTP clients.

questions.question: [TCS • Test 1 • Q10] What causes Thrashing in Operating System memory management?
options: CPU clock speed throttled due to temperature.
Network sockets buffer overflow.
Main memory is overloaded, causing the OS to spend more time swapping pages to disk than executing process instructions.
Deadlock among mutual exclusion locks.
questions.correctAnswer: Main memory is overloaded, causing the OS to spend more time swapping pages to disk than executing process instructions.
questions.explanation: Thrashing occurs when active working sets exceed physical RAM, causing continuous page faults and disk I/O thrashing.
questions.hint: Continuous page faults and disk swapping.
questions.relatedConcept: TCS - OS Virtual Memory & Page Replacement
questions.interviewTip: Working set model prevents thrashing by ensuring processes have sufficient page frames.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q1] What determines the memory alignment padding inserted by modern C compilers inside structs?
options: Always strictly packs bytes with zero gaps.
Aligns member offsets to multiples of member size (e.g. 8-byte boundary for double), padding struct to a multiple of largest member.
Aligns all variables to 64-byte cache line boundaries.
Padding depends only on operating system file system block size.
questions.correctAnswer: Aligns member offsets to multiples of member size (e.g. 8-byte boundary for double), padding struct to a multiple of largest member.
questions.explanation: CPUs read words faster when aligned to natural boundaries. The double member (8 bytes) requires 8-byte offset alignment.
questions.hint: Largest member alignment constraint dictates total struct sizing.
questions.relatedConcept: C - Struct Alignment & Padding
questions.interviewTip: Arrange struct members from largest to smallest to minimize padding waste.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q2] Why does executing '*ptr = 'Z';' on 'char *ptr = "Data";' crash with Segmentation Fault on Unix/Linux?
options: Heap memory was exhausted.
Pointer was null.
Pointers to char can only hold ASCII 0-127.
String literals are placed in read-only text (.rodata) memory segment by the linker.
questions.correctAnswer: String literals are placed in read-only text (.rodata) memory segment by the linker.
questions.explanation: Modifying write-protected memory pages causes the CPU memory management unit (MMU) to trigger a segmentation violation.
questions.hint: String literals live in read-only text segments.
questions.relatedConcept: C - String Literal Immutability
questions.interviewTip: Use 'char str[] = "Data";' to allocate mutable stack storage.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q3] When evaluating pointer expression '*(arr + 3)' where 'int arr[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};', what value is retrieved?
options: 30 (dereferences index 2).
40 (dereferences index 3 directly).
Address of arr[3].
Garbage memory value.
questions.correctAnswer: 40 (dereferences index 3 directly).
questions.explanation: *(arr + i) is mathematically identical to arr[i]. With offset 3, it fetches the 4th element (40).
questions.hint: arr[i] is defined as *(arr + i) in standard C.
questions.relatedConcept: C - Pointer Arithmetic & Array Strides
questions.interviewTip: Pointer subscript symmetry means 3[arr] is also valid C syntax!

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q4] What occurs if a function returns a pointer to a local stack array 'int local[10]' in C?
options: Stack frame is automatically preserved in heap.
Triggers a mandatory compiler abort.
Memory is promoted to static global scope.
Returns a dangling pointer to deallocated stack memory, causing undefined behavior on access.
questions.correctAnswer: Returns a dangling pointer to deallocated stack memory, causing undefined behavior on access.
questions.explanation: Stack frames are invalidated upon function return. Accessing returned stack pointers invokes undefined behavior.
questions.hint: Stack allocations are freed when function returns.
questions.relatedConcept: C - Dynamic Heap vs Stack Lifetime
questions.interviewTip: Always use malloc() or pass a buffer pointer from caller if data must outlive function execution.

questions.question: [C • Test 2 • Q5] Which bitwise operation toggles the k-th bit of an integer variable 'num' without altering other bits?
options: num ^= (1 << k) (XOR with a single-bit mask).
num = num >> k
questions.correctAnswer: num ^= (1 << k) (XOR with a single-bit mask).
questions.explanation: Bitwise XOR with 1 flips the bit (0->1, 1->0), while XOR with 0 preserves original bit state.
questions.hint: XOR with 1 toggles; OR sets; AND with NOT clears.
questions.relatedConcept: C - Bitwise Operators & Masking
questions.interviewTip: Bit manipulation is evaluated in all embedded, firmware, and low-level screening rounds.

title: Google - Test 2: Technical Assessment
description: Dynamic Test 2 for Google with 100% unique questions.

questions.question: [Google • Test 2 • Q1] What is the primary purpose of the Circuit Breaker pattern in microservice architecture?
options: Encrypts payload traffic with TLS.
Fails fast when downstream services become unresponsive, preventing cascading thread starvation across the system.
Balances network load across all containers.
Compresses JSON responses.
questions.correctAnswer: Fails fast when downstream services become unresponsive, preventing cascading thread starvation across the system.
questions.explanation: Circuit Breakers track failure rates and trip Open to reject requests immediately, returning fallback responses until health recovers.
questions.hint: Fails fast to protect system resilience.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - Microservices Circuit Breaker Pattern
questions.interviewTip: Always define fallbacks and reasonable timeout thresholds for HTTP clients.

questions.question: [Google • Test 2 • Q2] What causes Thrashing in Operating System memory management?
options: CPU clock speed throttled due to temperature.
Network sockets buffer overflow.
Deadlock among mutual exclusion locks.
Main memory is overloaded, causing the OS to spend more time swapping pages to disk than executing process instructions.
questions.correctAnswer: Main memory is overloaded, causing the OS to spend more time swapping pages to disk than executing process instructions.
questions.explanation: Thrashing occurs when active working sets exceed physical RAM, causing continuous page faults and disk I/O thrashing.
questions.hint: Continuous page faults and disk swapping.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - OS Virtual Memory & Page Replacement
questions.interviewTip: Working set model prevents thrashing by ensuring processes have sufficient page frames.

questions.question: [Google • Test 2 • Q3] What is the sequence of control flags exchanged during the standard TCP connection establishment?
options: ACK -> SYN -> FIN
SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK
SYN -> ACK -> DATA
RST -> SYN -> ACK
questions.correctAnswer: SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK
questions.explanation: Client sends SYN with initial sequence number (ISN), Server responds with SYN-ACK, Client sends ACK to establish full-duplex session.
questions.hint: Synchronize, Synchronize-Acknowledge, Acknowledge.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - TCP 3-Way Handshake & Flow Control
questions.interviewTip: TCP 3-way handshake sequence is a universal computer network interview question.

questions.question: [Google • Test 2 • Q4] In SOLID principles, what does the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) enforce?
options: Every class must inherit from exactly one parent.
Classes should be open for modification and closed for extension.
Dependencies must be hardcoded statically.
Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without altering program correctness.
questions.correctAnswer: Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without altering program correctness.
questions.explanation: LSP guarantees that derived classes honor the contract and behavior expectations established by the base type.
questions.hint: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - Object Oriented Design & SOLID Principles
questions.interviewTip: Violating LSP often occurs when overriding methods with empty implementations or unexpected exceptions.

questions.question: [Google • Test 2 • Q5] In Distributed Storage, how does Consistent Hashing minimize partition migration when a node is added?
options: Rehashes all keys across all servers from scratch.
Maps servers and keys to a 360-degree hash ring, so adding a node only migrates k/N keys from its immediate neighbor.
Duplicates all partitions to every machine in cluster.
Freezes all transactions until rebalancing completes.
questions.correctAnswer: Maps servers and keys to a 360-degree hash ring, so adding a node only migrates k/N keys from its immediate neighbor.
questions.explanation: Consistent Hashing ensures that only adjacent ring segments are redistributed, minimizing network transfer during cluster scaling.
questions.hint: Hash ring bounds key migration to immediate neighbors.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - Consistent Hashing in Distributed Systems
questions.interviewTip: Amazon DynamoDB and Cassandra use consistent hashing with virtual nodes.

questions.question: [Google • Test 2 • Q6] Which SQL transaction isolation level prevents Dirty Reads and Non-Repeatable Reads, but may allow Phantom Reads?
options: READ COMMITTED
READ UNCOMMITTED
SERIALIZABLE
REPEATABLE READ
questions.correctAnswer: REPEATABLE READ
questions.explanation: Repeatable Read locks scanned rows preventing updates, but standard SQL allows concurrent transactions to insert new matching rows (phantoms).
questions.hint: Read Uncommitted < Read Committed < Repeatable Read < Serializable.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - ACID Isolation & Concurrency Anomalies
questions.interviewTip: Serializable eliminates all anomalies via strict range locking or SSI.

questions.question: [Google • Test 2 • Q7] Why do database storage engines (InnoDB, Postgres) utilize B+ Trees instead of standard Binary Search Trees?
options: B+ Trees eliminate all disk writes.
High fan-out minimizes disk I/O depth (O(log_B N)), and linked leaf nodes allow sequential range scans.
Binary trees cannot store string keys.
B+ Trees automatically compress data in RAM.
questions.correctAnswer: High fan-out minimizes disk I/O depth (O(log_B N)), and linked leaf nodes allow sequential range scans.
questions.explanation: B+ Trees store records only in linked leaves. The wide branching factor (high fan-out) reduces tree height to 3-4 levels for millions of rows.
questions.hint: High fan-out reduces disk page reads.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - B+ Tree Indexing & Range Lookups
questions.interviewTip: Understand covering index (index-only scan) optimization for SQL queries.

options: 30 (dereferences index 2).
40 (dereferences index 3 directly).
Address of arr[3].
Garbage memory value.
questions.correctAnswer: 40 (dereferences index 3 directly).
questions.explanation: *(arr + i) is mathematically identical to arr[i]. With offset 3, it fetches the 4th element (40).
questions.hint: arr[i] is defined as *(arr + i) in standard C.
questions.relatedConcept: C - Pointer Arithmetic & Array Strides
questions.interviewTip: Pointer subscript symmetry means 3[arr] is also valid C syntax!

questions.question: [C • Test 4 • Q12] What occurs if a function returns a pointer to a local stack array 'int local[10]' in C?
options: Stack frame is automatically preserved in heap.
Triggers a mandatory compiler abort.
Memory is promoted to static global scope.
Returns a dangling pointer to deallocated stack memory, causing undefined behavior on access.
questions.correctAnswer: Returns a dangling pointer to deallocated stack memory, causing undefined behavior on access.
questions.explanation: Stack frames are invalidated upon function return. Accessing returned stack pointers invokes undefined behavior.
questions.hint: Stack allocations are freed when function returns.
questions.relatedConcept: C - Dynamic Heap vs Stack Lifetime
questions.interviewTip: Always use malloc() or pass a buffer pointer from caller if data must outlive function execution.

questions.question: [C • Test 4 • Q13] Which bitwise operation toggles the k-th bit of an integer variable 'num' without altering other bits?
options: num ^= (1 << k) (XOR with a single-bit mask).
num = num >> k
questions.correctAnswer: num ^= (1 << k) (XOR with a single-bit mask).
questions.explanation: Bitwise XOR with 1 flips the bit (0->1, 1->0), while XOR with 0 preserves original bit state.
questions.hint: XOR with 1 toggles; OR sets; AND with NOT clears.
questions.relatedConcept: C - Bitwise Operators & Masking
questions.interviewTip: Bit manipulation is evaluated in all embedded, firmware, and low-level screening rounds.

questions.question: [C • Test 4 • Q14] What determines the memory alignment padding inserted by modern C compilers inside structs?
options: Always strictly packs bytes with zero gaps.
Aligns all variables to 64-byte cache line boundaries.
Padding depends only on operating system file system block size.
Aligns member offsets to multiples of member size (e.g. 8-byte boundary for double), padding struct to a multiple of largest member.
questions.correctAnswer: Aligns member offsets to multiples of member size (e.g. 8-byte boundary for double), padding struct to a multiple of largest member.
questions.explanation: CPUs read words faster when aligned to natural boundaries. The double member (8 bytes) requires 8-byte offset alignment.
questions.hint: Largest member alignment constraint dictates total struct sizing.
questions.relatedConcept: C - Struct Alignment & Padding
questions.interviewTip: Arrange struct members from largest to smallest to minimize padding waste.

questions.question: [C • Test 4 • Q15] Why does executing '*ptr = 'Z';' on 'char *ptr = "Data";' crash with Segmentation Fault on Unix/Linux?
options: Heap memory was exhausted.
String literals are placed in read-only text (.rodata) memory segment by the linker.
Pointer was null.
Pointers to char can only hold ASCII 0-127.
questions.correctAnswer: String literals are placed in read-only text (.rodata) memory segment by the linker.
questions.explanation: Modifying write-protected memory pages causes the CPU memory management unit (MMU) to trigger a segmentation violation.
questions.hint: String literals live in read-only text segments.
questions.relatedConcept: C - String Literal Immutability
questions.interviewTip: Use 'char str[] = "Data";' to allocate mutable stack storage.

title: Google - Test 3: Technical Assessment
description: Dynamic Test 3 for Google with 100% unique questions.

questions.question: [Google • Test 3 • Q1] What causes Thrashing in Operating System memory management?
options: CPU clock speed throttled due to temperature.
Main memory is overloaded, causing the OS to spend more time swapping pages to disk than executing process instructions.
Network sockets buffer overflow.
Deadlock among mutual exclusion locks.
questions.correctAnswer: Main memory is overloaded, causing the OS to spend more time swapping pages to disk than executing process instructions.
questions.explanation: Thrashing occurs when active working sets exceed physical RAM, causing continuous page faults and disk I/O thrashing.
questions.hint: Continuous page faults and disk swapping.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - OS Virtual Memory & Page Replacement
questions.interviewTip: Working set model prevents thrashing by ensuring processes have sufficient page frames.

questions.question: [Google • Test 3 • Q2] What is the sequence of control flags exchanged during the standard TCP connection establishment?
options: ACK -> SYN -> FIN
SYN -> ACK -> DATA
RST -> SYN -> ACK
SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK
questions.correctAnswer: SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK
questions.explanation: Client sends SYN with initial sequence number (ISN), Server responds with SYN-ACK, Client sends ACK to establish full-duplex session.
questions.hint: Synchronize, Synchronize-Acknowledge, Acknowledge.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - TCP 3-Way Handshake & Flow Control
questions.interviewTip: TCP 3-way handshake sequence is a universal computer network interview question.

questions.question: [Google • Test 3 • Q3] In SOLID principles, what does the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) enforce?
options: Every class must inherit from exactly one parent.
Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without altering program correctness.
Classes should be open for modification and closed for extension.
Dependencies must be hardcoded statically.
questions.correctAnswer: Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without altering program correctness.
questions.explanation: LSP guarantees that derived classes honor the contract and behavior expectations established by the base type.
questions.hint: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - Object Oriented Design & SOLID Principles
questions.interviewTip: Violating LSP often occurs when overriding methods with empty implementations or unexpected exceptions.

questions.question: [Google • Test 3 • Q4] In Distributed Storage, how does Consistent Hashing minimize partition migration when a node is added?
options: Rehashes all keys across all servers from scratch.
Duplicates all partitions to every machine in cluster.
Freezes all transactions until rebalancing completes.
Maps servers and keys to a 360-degree hash ring, so adding a node only migrates k/N keys from its immediate neighbor.
questions.correctAnswer: Maps servers and keys to a 360-degree hash ring, so adding a node only migrates k/N keys from its immediate neighbor.
questions.explanation: Consistent Hashing ensures that only adjacent ring segments are redistributed, minimizing network transfer during cluster scaling.
questions.hint: Hash ring bounds key migration to immediate neighbors.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - Consistent Hashing in Distributed Systems
questions.interviewTip: Amazon DynamoDB and Cassandra use consistent hashing with virtual nodes.

questions.question: [Google • Test 3 • Q5] Which SQL transaction isolation level prevents Dirty Reads and Non-Repeatable Reads, but may allow Phantom Reads?
options: READ COMMITTED
REPEATABLE READ
READ UNCOMMITTED
SERIALIZABLE
questions.correctAnswer: REPEATABLE READ
questions.explanation: Repeatable Read locks scanned rows preventing updates, but standard SQL allows concurrent transactions to insert new matching rows (phantoms).
questions.hint: Read Uncommitted < Read Committed < Repeatable Read < Serializable.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - ACID Isolation & Concurrency Anomalies
questions.interviewTip: Serializable eliminates all anomalies via strict range locking or SSI.

questions.question: [Google • Test 3 • Q6] Why do database storage engines (InnoDB, Postgres) utilize B+ Trees instead of standard Binary Search Trees?
options: B+ Trees eliminate all disk writes.
Binary trees cannot store string keys.
B+ Trees automatically compress data in RAM.
High fan-out minimizes disk I/O depth (O(log_B N)), and linked leaf nodes allow sequential range scans.
questions.correctAnswer: High fan-out minimizes disk I/O depth (O(log_B N)), and linked leaf nodes allow sequential range scans.
questions.explanation: B+ Trees store records only in linked leaves. The wide branching factor (high fan-out) reduces tree height to 3-4 levels for millions of rows.
questions.hint: High fan-out reduces disk page reads.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - B+ Tree Indexing & Range Lookups
questions.interviewTip: Understand covering index (index-only scan) optimization for SQL queries.

questions.question: [Google • Test 3 • Q7] What is the primary purpose of the Circuit Breaker pattern in microservice architecture?
options: Encrypts payload traffic with TLS.
Fails fast when downstream services become unresponsive, preventing cascading thread starvation across the system.
Balances network load across all containers.
Compresses JSON responses.
questions.correctAnswer: Fails fast when downstream services become unresponsive, preventing cascading thread starvation across the system.
questions.explanation: Circuit Breakers track failure rates and trip Open to reject requests immediately, returning fallback responses until health recovers.
questions.hint: Fails fast to protect system resilience.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - Microservices Circuit Breaker Pattern
questions.interviewTip: Always define fallbacks and reasonable timeout thresholds for HTTP clients.

title: Google - Test 4: Technical Assessment
description: Dynamic Test 4 for Google with 100% unique questions.

questions.question: [Google • Test 4 • Q1] What is the sequence of control flags exchanged during the standard TCP connection establishment?
options: ACK -> SYN -> FIN
SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK
SYN -> ACK -> DATA
RST -> SYN -> ACK
questions.correctAnswer: SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK
questions.explanation: Client sends SYN with initial sequence number (ISN), Server responds with SYN-ACK, Client sends ACK to establish full-duplex session.
questions.hint: Synchronize, Synchronize-Acknowledge, Acknowledge.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - TCP 3-Way Handshake & Flow Control
questions.interviewTip: TCP 3-way handshake sequence is a universal computer network interview question.

questions.question: [Google • Test 4 • Q2] In SOLID principles, what does the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) enforce?
options: Every class must inherit from exactly one parent.
Classes should be open for modification and closed for extension.
Dependencies must be hardcoded statically.
Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without altering program correctness.
questions.correctAnswer: Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without altering program correctness.
questions.explanation: LSP guarantees that derived classes honor the contract and behavior expectations established by the base type.
questions.hint: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - Object Oriented Design & SOLID Principles
questions.interviewTip: Violating LSP often occurs when overriding methods with empty implementations or unexpected exceptions.

questions.question: [Google • Test 4 • Q3] In Distributed Storage, how does Consistent Hashing minimize partition migration when a node is added?
options: Rehashes all keys across all servers from scratch.
Maps servers and keys to a 360-degree hash ring, so adding a node only migrates k/N keys from its immediate neighbor.
Duplicates all partitions to every machine in cluster.
Freezes all transactions until rebalancing completes.
questions.correctAnswer: Maps servers and keys to a 360-degree hash ring, so adding a node only migrates k/N keys from its immediate neighbor.
questions.explanation: Consistent Hashing ensures that only adjacent ring segments are redistributed, minimizing network transfer during cluster scaling.
questions.hint: Hash ring bounds key migration to immediate neighbors.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - Consistent Hashing in Distributed Systems
questions.interviewTip: Amazon DynamoDB and Cassandra use consistent hashing with virtual nodes.

questions.question: [Google • Test 4 • Q4] Which SQL transaction isolation level prevents Dirty Reads and Non-Repeatable Reads, but may allow Phantom Reads?
options: READ COMMITTED
READ UNCOMMITTED
SERIALIZABLE
REPEATABLE READ
questions.correctAnswer: REPEATABLE READ
questions.explanation: Repeatable Read locks scanned rows preventing updates, but standard SQL allows concurrent transactions to insert new matching rows (phantoms).
questions.hint: Read Uncommitted < Read Committed < Repeatable Read < Serializable.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - ACID Isolation & Concurrency Anomalies
questions.interviewTip: Serializable eliminates all anomalies via strict range locking or SSI.

questions.question: [Google • Test 4 • Q5] Why do database storage engines (InnoDB, Postgres) utilize B+ Trees instead of standard Binary Search Trees?
options: B+ Trees eliminate all disk writes.
High fan-out minimizes disk I/O depth (O(log_B N)), and linked leaf nodes allow sequential range scans.
Binary trees cannot store string keys.
B+ Trees automatically compress data in RAM.
questions.correctAnswer: High fan-out minimizes disk I/O depth (O(log_B N)), and linked leaf nodes allow sequential range scans.
questions.explanation: B+ Trees store records only in linked leaves. The wide branching factor (high fan-out) reduces tree height to 3-4 levels for millions of rows.
questions.hint: High fan-out reduces disk page reads.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - B+ Tree Indexing & Range Lookups
questions.interviewTip: Understand covering index (index-only scan) optimization for SQL queries.

questions.question: [Google • Test 4 • Q6] What is the primary purpose of the Circuit Breaker pattern in microservice architecture?
options: Encrypts payload traffic with TLS.
Balances network load across all containers.
Compresses JSON responses.
Fails fast when downstream services become unresponsive, preventing cascading thread starvation across the system.
questions.correctAnswer: Fails fast when downstream services become unresponsive, preventing cascading thread starvation across the system.
questions.explanation: Circuit Breakers track failure rates and trip Open to reject requests immediately, returning fallback responses until health recovers.
questions.hint: Fails fast to protect system resilience.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - Microservices Circuit Breaker Pattern
questions.interviewTip: Always define fallbacks and reasonable timeout thresholds for HTTP clients.

questions.question: [Google • Test 4 • Q7] What causes Thrashing in Operating System memory management?
options: CPU clock speed throttled due to temperature.
Main memory is overloaded, causing the OS to spend more time swapping pages to disk than executing process instructions.
Network sockets buffer overflow.
Deadlock among mutual exclusion locks.
questions.correctAnswer: Main memory is overloaded, causing the OS to spend more time swapping pages to disk than executing process instructions.
questions.explanation: Thrashing occurs when active working sets exceed physical RAM, causing continuous page faults and disk I/O thrashing.
questions.hint: Continuous page faults and disk swapping.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - OS Virtual Memory & Page Replacement
questions.interviewTip: Working set model prevents thrashing by ensuring processes have sufficient page frames.

questions.question: [C • Test 8 • Q1] Why does executing '*ptr = 'Z';' on 'char *ptr = "Data";' crash with Segmentation Fault on Unix/Linux?

questions.question: [Google • Test 5 • Q1] In SOLID principles, what does the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) enforce?
options: Every class must inherit from exactly one parent.
Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without altering program correctness.
Classes should be open for modification and closed for extension.
Dependencies must be hardcoded statically.
questions.correctAnswer: Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without altering program correctness.
questions.explanation: LSP guarantees that derived classes honor the contract and behavior expectations established by the base type.
questions.hint: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - Object Oriented Design & SOLID Principles
questions.interviewTip: Violating LSP often occurs when overriding methods with empty implementations or unexpected exceptions.

questions.question: [Google • Test 5 • Q2] In Distributed Storage, how does Consistent Hashing minimize partition migration when a node is added?
options: Rehashes all keys across all servers from scratch.
Duplicates all partitions to every machine in cluster.
Freezes all transactions until rebalancing completes.
Maps servers and keys to a 360-degree hash ring, so adding a node only migrates k/N keys from its immediate neighbor.
questions.correctAnswer: Maps servers and keys to a 360-degree hash ring, so adding a node only migrates k/N keys from its immediate neighbor.
questions.explanation: Consistent Hashing ensures that only adjacent ring segments are redistributed, minimizing network transfer during cluster scaling.
questions.hint: Hash ring bounds key migration to immediate neighbors.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - Consistent Hashing in Distributed Systems
questions.interviewTip: Amazon DynamoDB and Cassandra use consistent hashing with virtual nodes.

questions.question: [Google • Test 5 • Q3] Which SQL transaction isolation level prevents Dirty Reads and Non-Repeatable Reads, but may allow Phantom Reads?
options: READ COMMITTED
REPEATABLE READ
READ UNCOMMITTED
SERIALIZABLE
questions.correctAnswer: REPEATABLE READ
questions.explanation: Repeatable Read locks scanned rows preventing updates, but standard SQL allows concurrent transactions to insert new matching rows (phantoms).
questions.hint: Read Uncommitted < Read Committed < Repeatable Read < Serializable.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - ACID Isolation & Concurrency Anomalies
questions.interviewTip: Serializable eliminates all anomalies via strict range locking or SSI.

questions.question: [Google • Test 5 • Q4] Why do database storage engines (InnoDB, Postgres) utilize B+ Trees instead of standard Binary Search Trees?
options: B+ Trees eliminate all disk writes.
Binary trees cannot store string keys.
B+ Trees automatically compress data in RAM.
High fan-out minimizes disk I/O depth (O(log_B N)), and linked leaf nodes allow sequential range scans.
questions.correctAnswer: High fan-out minimizes disk I/O depth (O(log_B N)), and linked leaf nodes allow sequential range scans.
questions.explanation: B+ Trees store records only in linked leaves. The wide branching factor (high fan-out) reduces tree height to 3-4 levels for millions of rows.
questions.hint: High fan-out reduces disk page reads.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - B+ Tree Indexing & Range Lookups
questions.interviewTip: Understand covering index (index-only scan) optimization for SQL queries.

questions.question: [Google • Test 5 • Q5] What is the primary purpose of the Circuit Breaker pattern in microservice architecture?
options: Encrypts payload traffic with TLS.
Fails fast when downstream services become unresponsive, preventing cascading thread starvation across the system.
Balances network load across all containers.
Compresses JSON responses.
questions.correctAnswer: Fails fast when downstream services become unresponsive, preventing cascading thread starvation across the system.
questions.explanation: Circuit Breakers track failure rates and trip Open to reject requests immediately, returning fallback responses until health recovers.
questions.hint: Fails fast to protect system resilience.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - Microservices Circuit Breaker Pattern
questions.interviewTip: Always define fallbacks and reasonable timeout thresholds for HTTP clients.

questions.question: [Google • Test 5 • Q6] What causes Thrashing in Operating System memory management?
options: CPU clock speed throttled due to temperature.
Network sockets buffer overflow.
Deadlock among mutual exclusion locks.
Main memory is overloaded, causing the OS to spend more time swapping pages to disk than executing process instructions.
questions.correctAnswer: Main memory is overloaded, causing the OS to spend more time swapping pages to disk than executing process instructions.
questions.explanation: Thrashing occurs when active working sets exceed physical RAM, causing continuous page faults and disk I/O thrashing.
questions.hint: Continuous page faults and disk swapping.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - OS Virtual Memory & Page Replacement
questions.interviewTip: Working set model prevents thrashing by ensuring processes have sufficient page frames.

Maps servers and keys to a 360-degree hash ring, so adding a node only migrates k/N keys from its immediate neighbor.
Duplicates all partitions to every machine in cluster.
Freezes all transactions until rebalancing completes.
questions.correctAnswer: Maps servers and keys to a 360-degree hash ring, so adding a node only migrates k/N keys from its immediate neighbor.
questions.explanation: Consistent Hashing ensures that only adjacent ring segments are redistributed, minimizing network transfer during cluster scaling.
questions.hint: Hash ring bounds key migration to immediate neighbors.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - Consistent Hashing in Distributed Systems
questions.interviewTip: Amazon DynamoDB and Cassandra use consistent hashing with virtual nodes.

questions.question: [Google • Test 5 • Q10] Which SQL transaction isolation level prevents Dirty Reads and Non-Repeatable Reads, but may allow Phantom Reads?
options: READ COMMITTED
READ UNCOMMITTED
SERIALIZABLE
REPEATABLE READ
questions.correctAnswer: REPEATABLE READ
questions.explanation: Repeatable Read locks scanned rows preventing updates, but standard SQL allows concurrent transactions to insert new matching rows (phantoms).
questions.hint: Read Uncommitted < Read Committed < Repeatable Read < Serializable.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - ACID Isolation & Concurrency Anomalies
questions.interviewTip: Serializable eliminates all anomalies via strict range locking or SSI.

questions.question: [Google • Test 5 • Q11] Why do database storage engines (InnoDB, Postgres) utilize B+ Trees instead of standard Binary Search Trees?
options: B+ Trees eliminate all disk writes.
High fan-out minimizes disk I/O depth (O(log_B N)), and linked leaf nodes allow sequential range scans.
Binary trees cannot store string keys.
B+ Trees automatically compress data in RAM.
questions.correctAnswer: High fan-out minimizes disk I/O depth (O(log_B N)), and linked leaf nodes allow sequential range scans.
questions.explanation: B+ Trees store records only in linked leaves. The wide branching factor (high fan-out) reduces tree height to 3-4 levels for millions of rows.
questions.hint: High fan-out reduces disk page reads.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - B+ Tree Indexing & Range Lookups
questions.interviewTip: Understand covering index (index-only scan) optimization for SQL queries.

questions.question: [Google • Test 5 • Q12] What is the primary purpose of the Circuit Breaker pattern in microservice architecture?
options: Encrypts payload traffic with TLS.
Balances network load across all containers.
Compresses JSON responses.
Fails fast when downstream services become unresponsive, preventing cascading thread starvation across the system.
questions.correctAnswer: Fails fast when downstream services become unresponsive, preventing cascading thread starvation across the system.
questions.explanation: Circuit Breakers track failure rates and trip Open to reject requests immediately, returning fallback responses until health recovers.
questions.hint: Fails fast to protect system resilience.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - Microservices Circuit Breaker Pattern
questions.interviewTip: Always define fallbacks and reasonable timeout thresholds for HTTP clients.

questions.question: [Google • Test 5 • Q13] What causes Thrashing in Operating System memory management?
options: CPU clock speed throttled due to temperature.
Main memory is overloaded, causing the OS to spend more time swapping pages to disk than executing process instructions.
Network sockets buffer overflow.
Deadlock among mutual exclusion locks.
questions.correctAnswer: Main memory is overloaded, causing the OS to spend more time swapping pages to disk than executing process instructions.
questions.explanation: Thrashing occurs when active working sets exceed physical RAM, causing continuous page faults and disk I/O thrashing.
questions.hint: Continuous page faults and disk swapping.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - OS Virtual Memory & Page Replacement
questions.interviewTip: Working set model prevents thrashing by ensuring processes have sufficient page frames.

questions.question: [Google • Test 5 • Q14] What is the sequence of control flags exchanged during the standard TCP connection establishment?
options: ACK -> SYN -> FIN
SYN -> ACK -> DATA
RST -> SYN -> ACK
SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK
questions.correctAnswer: SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK
questions.explanation: Client sends SYN with initial sequence number (ISN), Server responds with SYN-ACK, Client sends ACK to establish full-duplex session.
questions.hint: Synchronize, Synchronize-Acknowledge, Acknowledge.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - TCP 3-Way Handshake & Flow Control
questions.interviewTip: TCP 3-way handshake sequence is a universal computer network interview question.

questions.question: [Google • Test 5 • Q15] In SOLID principles, what does the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) enforce?
options: Every class must inherit from exactly one parent.
Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without altering program correctness.
Classes should be open for modification and closed for extension.
Dependencies must be hardcoded statically.
questions.correctAnswer: Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without altering program correctness.
questions.explanation: LSP guarantees that derived classes honor the contract and behavior expectations established by the base type.
questions.hint: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types.
questions.relatedConcept: Google - Object Oriented Design & SOLID Principles
questions.interviewTip: Violating LSP often occurs when overriding methods with empty implementations or unexpected exceptions.

questions.question: What is the standard behavior when `longjmp()` is invoked from a nested function call, provided the corresponding `setjmp()` was called in an outer function that has already returned?
options: Undefined behavior, typically resulting in corruption of the call stack or a segmentation fault.
The program cleanly exits with code 1.
It safely resets execution back to the `setjmp` call site inside `outer`.
A compilation error due to stack frame mismatch.
questions.correctAnswer: Undefined behavior, typically resulting in corruption of the call stack or a segmentation fault.
questions.explanation: Invoking `longjmp` after the function that invoked `setjmp` has returned execution destroys the target stack frame context, leading to undefined behavior.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to local stack frames when functions exit.
questions.relatedConcept: Non-local jumps and stack lifetime
questions.interviewTip: Always ensure `setjmp` scopes outlive any matching `longjmp` calls.

questions.question: How does the `restrict` keyword, introduced in C99, affect pointer analysis and compiler optimizations?
options: It guarantees that the pointers are the sole initial means of referencing the memory objects they point to within their scope, enabling aggressive load/store optimizations.
It makes the pointers thread-safe by enforcing atomic memory operations.
It restricts pointer arithmetic, preventing out-of-bounds index errors at runtime.
It enforces that the pointer can only be read from and never written to.
questions.correctAnswer: It guarantees that the pointers are the sole initial means of referencing the memory objects they point to within their scope, enabling aggressive load/store optimizations.
questions.explanation: The `restrict` type qualifier tells the compiler that for the lifetime of the pointer, only it (or a derivative) will be used to access the object it points to, allowing the compiler to optimize without worrying about aliasing.
questions.hint: Think about pointer aliasing and how compilers optimize loops and memory access.
questions.relatedConcept: Pointer Aliasing and Restrict Qualifier
questions.interviewTip: Mention alias analysis when discussing performance tuning in C.

questions.question: What is the output or behavior of the following C code snippet utilizing flexible array members?
options: It prints the size of `int` (typically 4) or slightly more with padding, because flexible array members contribute zero bytes to `sizeof` of the structure.
It prints 14, accounting for the `int` plus the 10 flexible chars.
It results in a compilation error because flexible array members cannot be used with `malloc`.
It prints 0 because the structure has no fixed members.
questions.correctAnswer: It prints the size of `int` (typically 4) or slightly more with padding, because flexible array members contribute zero bytes to `sizeof` of the structure.
questions.explanation: Flexible array members allow a struct to have a trailing array of unspecified size. They do not occupy space in the `sizeof` operator evaluation.
questions.hint: Consider how `sizeof` handles trailing arrays with no explicit dimension inside a struct.
questions.relatedConcept: Flexible Array Members
questions.interviewTip: Flexible array members are a standard C99 idiom for implementing variable-length buffers inside structs.

questions.question: In the context of C preprocessor macros, what is the primary pitfall of the following macro definition?
options: Operator precedence issues when expressions are passed as arguments (e.g., SQUARE(1 + 2) expands to 1 + 2 * 1 + 2 instead of (1+2)*(1+2)).
It causes syntax errors if `x` is of type `float` or `double`.
It results in multiple evaluations of `x` causing side effects if expressions like `SQUARE(i++)` are used.
Both A and C are correct.
questions.correctAnswer: Both A and C are correct.
questions.explanation: Unparenthesized macro parameters cause operator precedence bugs, and side-effect expressions (like increment operators) get evaluated multiple times, making both A and C valid issues.
questions.hint: Look at what happens if you pass an expression with operators or side-effects.
questions.relatedConcept: Preprocessor Macro Pitfalls
questions.interviewTip: Always wrap macro arguments and the macro body itself in parentheses, or prefer `static inline` functions.

questions.question: What is the execution outcome of the following snippet involving compound literals?
options: It prints 0, but accessing `p` afterwards outside `get_origin` is technically undefined behavior because compound literals defined inside functions have block scope.
It prints 0 securely because compound literals have static storage duration by default.
It fails to compile because taking the address of a compound literal is illegal.
It causes a segmentation fault immediately during assignment.
questions.correctAnswer: It prints 0, but accessing `p` afterwards outside `get_origin` is technically undefined behavior because compound literals defined inside functions have block scope.
questions.explanation: Compound literals have block scope when defined inside a function. Returning their address results in a dangling pointer once the block scope exits.
questions.hint: Think about the lifetime of compound literals declared inside block scopes.
questions.relatedConcept: Compound Literals and Storage Duration
questions.interviewTip: Compound literals at file scope have static duration, but inside functions, their lifetime is tied to the block.

questions.question: Which of the following statements accurately describes the behavior of `fflush()` when applied to an input stream (such as `stdin`) in standard C?
options: The behavior is undefined according to the C standard.
It successfully clears all remaining characters from the input buffer.
It resets the file position indicator to the beginning of the stream.
It blocks execution until the user presses Enter.
questions.correctAnswer: The behavior is undefined according to the C standard.
questions.explanation: The C standard specifies `fflush` for output streams. Using it on input streams is undefined behavior, although some compilers/libraries implement specific extensions.
questions.hint: Recall what the C standard says about flushing input streams vs output streams.
questions.relatedConcept: Stream I/O and Standard Behavior
questions.interviewTip: Never rely on `fflush(stdin)` for input clearing; use manual loops with `getchar()` instead.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the `volatile` keyword in embedded or concurrent C programming?
options: It prevents the compiler from optimizing out seemingly redundant reads or writes, ensuring every access goes directly to physical memory or hardware registers.
It ensures that the variable is stored in thread-local storage across multiple threads.
It makes operations on the variable atomic without requiring mutex locks.
It protects the memory region from being swapped out to disk.
questions.correctAnswer: It prevents the compiler from optimizing out seemingly redundant reads or writes, ensuring every access goes directly to physical memory or hardware registers.
questions.explanation: `volatile` informs the compiler that the value can be changed by entities outside the control of the program (like hardware or interrupts), disabling memory access optimizations.
questions.hint: Think about memory-mapped I/O and compiler optimization loops.
questions.relatedConcept: Volatile Qualifier and Hardware Registers
questions.interviewTip: Remember that `volatile` deals with visibility and optimization, NOT atomicity or thread safety.

questions.question: What does the `sig_atomic_t` type guarantee in signal-handling contexts?
options: Access to objects of type `sig_atomic_t` can be performed atomically, without the possibility of reading or writing half-updated values.
It guarantees that the variable is protected by a hardware-level spinlock.
It forces the compiler to allocate the variable in CPU registers exclusively.
It allows safe execution of multi-threaded thread pools within signal handlers.
questions.correctAnswer: Access to objects of type `sig_atomic_t` can be performed atomically, without the possibility of reading or writing half-updated values.
questions.explanation: `sig_atomic_t` is guaranteed to be read or written in a single uninterrupted operation, making it safe to modify in a signal handler and read in the main program (especially when combined with `volatile`).
questions.hint: Consider interrupt and signal safety when modifying variables shared with signal handlers.
questions.relatedConcept: Signal Safety and sig_atomic_t
questions.interviewTip: Always mark shared signal flags as `volatile sig_atomic_t`.

questions.question: What is the behavior of the following code snippet regarding pointer arithmetic on `void *`?
options: It is a GNU C extension allowing arithmetic on `void *` by treating the size as 1 byte, but it is technically non-standard ISO C.
It fails to compile in standard C because the size of `void` is incomplete.
It advances the pointer by `sizeof(int)` bytes.
It advances the pointer by exactly 4 bytes on all architectures regardless of extensions.
questions.correctAnswer: It is a GNU C extension allowing arithmetic on `void *` by treating the size as 1 byte, but it is technically non-standard ISO C.
questions.explanation: ISO C forbids pointer arithmetic on pointers to incomplete types like `void`. However, GCC/Clang allow it as an extension where `sizeof(void)` is treated as 1.
questions.hint: Check what standard ISO C says about `sizeof(void)` and pointer arithmetic.
questions.relatedConcept: Pointer Arithmetic on Void Pointers
questions.interviewTip: To remain strictly portable, always cast `void *` to `char *` before performing arithmetic.

questions.question: What is the output of the following program involving promotion rules and bitwise operations?
options: 0xF7 or equivalent bit pattern after integer promotion and truncation.
0x7F
0x8F
questions.correctAnswer: 0xF7 or equivalent bit pattern after integer promotion and truncation.
questions.explanation: `a` is promoted to `int` during `~a` (~0x00000080 = 0xFFFFFF7F). Shifting right by 4 gives 0x0FFFFF7. Cast/truncation back to `unsigned char` results in 0xF7.
questions.hint: Remember that integer promotion (`int` promotion) happens to operands smaller than `int` before bitwise operations.
questions.relatedConcept: Integer Promotions and Bitwise Operators
questions.interviewTip: Be extremely careful with bitwise operations on `char` or `short` due to implicit integer promotions.

questions.question: Which of the following functions from the standard library performs a binary search on a sorted array?
questions.codeSnippet: void *bsearch(const void *key, const void *base, size_t nitems, size_t size, int (*compar)(const void *, const void *));
options: `bsearch`
`qsort_search`
`binsearch`
`search_sorted`
questions.correctAnswer: `bsearch`
questions.explanation: `bsearch` is the standard library function defined in `<stdlib.h>` for performing binary searches on sorted arrays.
questions.hint: Look for the function name that matches the binary search abbreviation in `<stdlib.h>.
questions.relatedConcept: Standard Library Algorithms (bsearch)
questions.interviewTip: Ensure the array is fully sorted according to the exact same comparison function before calling `bsearch`.

questions.question: What is the correct declaration for a function pointer `func_ptr` that accepts an integer and a pointer to a character, and returns a pointer to a function which takes no arguments and returns `void`?
questions.codeSnippet: // What is the correct syntax signature?
options: void (*func_ptr(int, char *))(void);
void (*(*func_ptr)(int, char *))(void);
void *func_ptr(int, char *)();
void (*func_ptr)(int, char *)->void;
questions.correctAnswer: void (*(*func_ptr)(int, char *))(void);
questions.explanation: `func_ptr` is a pointer (`*func_ptr`) to a function taking `(int, char *)` and returning a pointer `void (*)(void)` to another function.
questions.hint: Use the 'spiral rule' or break it down inside out: a pointer to a function returning a function pointer.
questions.relatedConcept: Complex Function Pointers
questions.interviewTip: Use `typedef` for complex function pointers to greatly improve readability.

questions.question: What is the behavior of calling `realloc(ptr, 0)` when `ptr` is a valid pointer allocated previously on the heap?
options: It frees the memory pointed to by `ptr` and returns either `NULL` or a unique pointer that can be passed to `free`.
It leaves the memory untouched and returns `ptr`.
It causes undefined behavior because size cannot be zero.
It truncates the buffer size to 0 bytes without freeing the underlying block.
questions.correctAnswer: It frees the memory pointed to by `ptr` and returns either `NULL` or a unique pointer that can be passed to `free`.
questions.explanation: According to the C standard, passing 0 as the new size to `realloc` is equivalent to calling `free(ptr)`. It may return `NULL` or a pointer that must be freed.
questions.hint: Check the C standard behavior for `realloc` when the size argument is zero.
questions.relatedConcept: Memory Management (`realloc` edge cases)
questions.interviewTip: Modern coding guidelines recommend avoiding `realloc(ptr, 0)` for clarity; use explicit `free()` instead.

questions.question: What does the `offsetof` macro from `<stddef.h>` calculate?
options: The offset in bytes from the beginning of a structure to a given member.
The total memory size including padding of the structure.
The alignment requirement of the specified structure member.
The index of the member if the structure is treated as an array.
questions.correctAnswer: The offset in bytes from the beginning of a structure to a given member.
questions.explanation: `offsetof(type, member)` expands to an integer constant of type `size_t` that specifies the offset in bytes of the member from the beginning of the structure.
questions.hint: Think about low-level container-of macros and struct layouts.
questions.relatedConcept: Struct Layout and `offsetof`
questions.interviewTip: `offsetof` is heavily used in Linux kernel programming to implement container-of macros.

questions.question: What is the output of the following program involving string literal concatenation and array sizing?
questions.explanation: Adjacent string literals are automatically concatenated by the compiler into a single string: `"Hello World"`. Its length is 11 characters plus 1 null terminator, making `sizeof(str)` equal to 12.
questions.hint: Adjacent string literals in C are concatenated at translation phase 6.
questions.relatedConcept: String Literal Concatenation
questions.interviewTip: Remember that `sizeof` on character arrays includes the implicit null terminator byte.

questions.question: [C • Test 12 • Q1] What determines the memory alignment padding inserted by modern C compilers inside structs?
options: Aligns member offsets to multiples of member size (e.g. 8-byte boundary for double), padding struct to a multiple of largest member.
Always strictly packs bytes with zero gaps.
Aligns all variables to 64-byte cache line boundaries.
Padding depends only on operating system file system block size.
questions.correctAnswer: Aligns member offsets to multiples of member size (e.g. 8-byte boundary for double), padding struct to a multiple of largest member.
questions.explanation: CPUs read words faster when aligned to natural boundaries. The double member (8 bytes) requires 8-byte offset alignment.
questions.hint: Largest member alignment constraint dictates total struct sizing.
questions.relatedConcept: C - Struct Alignment & Padding
questions.interviewTip: Arrange struct members from largest to smallest to minimize padding waste.

questions.question: [C • Test 12 • Q2] Why does executing '*ptr = 'Z';' on 'char *ptr = "Data";' crash with Segmentation Fault on Unix/Linux?
options: Heap memory was exhausted.
Pointer was null.
String literals are placed in read-only text (.rodata) memory segment by the linker.
Pointers to char can only hold ASCII 0-127.
questions.correctAnswer: String literals are placed in read-only text (.rodata) memory segment by the linker.
questions.explanation: Modifying write-protected memory pages causes the CPU memory management unit (MMU) to trigger a segmentation violation.
questions.hint: String literals live in read-only text segments.
questions.relatedConcept: C - String Literal Immutability
questions.interviewTip: Use 'char str[] = "Data";' to allocate mutable stack storage.

questions.question: [C • Test 12 • Q3] When evaluating pointer expression '*(arr + 3)' where 'int arr[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};', what value is retrieved?
options: 40 (dereferences index 3 directly).
30 (dereferences index 2).
Address of arr[3].
Garbage memory value.
questions.correctAnswer: 40 (dereferences index 3 directly).
questions.explanation: *(arr + i) is mathematically identical to arr[i]. With offset 3, it fetches the 4th element (40).
questions.hint: arr[i] is defined as *(arr + i) in standard C.
questions.relatedConcept: C - Pointer Arithmetic & Array Strides
questions.interviewTip: Pointer subscript symmetry means 3[arr] is also valid C syntax!

questions.question: [C • Test 12 • Q4] What occurs if a function returns a pointer to a local stack array 'int local[10]' in C?
options: Stack frame is automatically preserved in heap.
Triggers a mandatory compiler abort.
Returns a dangling pointer to deallocated stack memory, causing undefined behavior on access.
Memory is promoted to static global scope.
questions.correctAnswer: Returns a dangling pointer to deallocated stack memory, causing undefined behavior on access.
questions.explanation: Stack frames are invalidated upon function return. Accessing returned stack pointers invokes undefined behavior.
questions.hint: Stack allocations are freed when function returns.
questions.relatedConcept: C - Dynamic Heap vs Stack Lifetime
questions.interviewTip: Always use malloc() or pass a buffer pointer from caller if data must outlive function execution.

num = num >> k
questions.correctAnswer: num ^= (1 << k) (XOR with a single-bit mask).
questions.explanation: Bitwise XOR with 1 flips the bit (0->1, 1->0), while XOR with 0 preserves original bit state.
questions.hint: XOR with 1 toggles; OR sets; AND with NOT clears.
questions.relatedConcept: C - Bitwise Operators & Masking
questions.interviewTip: Bit manipulation is evaluated in all embedded, firmware, and low-level screening rounds.

questions.question: [Python • Test 2 • Q1] What is the primary advantage of using a generator expression '(x*2 for x in data)' over list comprehension '[x*2 for x in data]'?
options: Generators evaluate lazily on-demand using O(1) memory, avoiding allocating the full list in RAM.
Generators execute 100x faster on GPU.
List comprehensions cannot be iterated in for loops.
Generators automatically save output to disk.
questions.correctAnswer: Generators evaluate lazily on-demand using O(1) memory, avoiding allocating the full list in RAM.
questions.explanation: Generators yield items one at a time using iterator protocol, making them essential for processing gigabyte-scale datasets.
questions.hint: Lazy evaluation saves RAM.
questions.relatedConcept: Python - Generator Memory Efficiency
questions.interviewTip: Generators are ideal for streaming log files or continuous database cursor streams.

questions.question: [Python • Test 2 • Q2] What is the output of calling 'def fn(val, acc=[]): acc.append(val); return acc' twice with fn(1) then fn(2)?
questions.codeSnippet:
def fn(val, acc=[]):
    acc.append(val)
    return acc
print(fn(1))
print(fn(2))
options: [1] then [2]
[1] then [1, 2] (default list object is bound ONCE at function definition time).
TypeError: default argument modified
questions.correctAnswer: [1] then [1, 2] (default list object is bound ONCE at function definition time).
questions.explanation: Default parameter values are evaluated once when def executes. The same list object is shared across subsequent invocations.
questions.hint: Use 'acc=None' inside function signature to create fresh default lists.
questions.relatedConcept: Python - Mutable Default Arguments
questions.interviewTip: Always use None as default value for mutable arguments in Python.

questions.question: [Python • Test 2 • Q3] How does the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) impact multithreading in CPython?
options: Restricts execution of Python bytecode to a single native thread at a time, limiting CPU-bound speedup across multiple cores.
Prevents memory leaks during asyncio coroutines.
Enforces static types on all global variables.
Bans socket networking over multiple threads.
questions.correctAnswer: Restricts execution of Python bytecode to a single native thread at a time, limiting CPU-bound speedup across multiple cores.
questions.explanation: GIL protects CPython memory management. CPU-bound code requires multiprocessing to achieve true multi-core parallelism.
questions.hint: One thread executes bytecode at a time in CPython.
questions.relatedConcept: Python - GIL & Concurrency Boundaries
questions.interviewTip: Use multiprocessing for CPU heavy tasks, threading/asyncio for I/O bound tasks.

title: Android App Development - Test 1: Core Fundamentals & Patterns
description: Comprehensive technical evaluation for Android App Development covering runtime mechanics, design principles, and problem solving.

questions.question: [Android App Development • Test 1 • Q1] In Android, what happens to an Activity during a screen orientation change by default?
options: The View tree is scaled without touching Activity lifecycle.
The Activity is destroyed and recreated (onDestroy -> onCreate), resetting unpersisted UI state.
The Activity enters onPause and freezes in memory.
Android OS crashes if orientation is unlocked.
questions.correctAnswer: The Activity is destroyed and recreated (onDestroy -> onCreate), resetting unpersisted UI state.
questions.explanation: Orientation changes trigger configuration change restarts. Architecture Components (ViewModel) retain UI state across Activity recreation.
questions.hint: Destroyed and recreated; ViewModel preserves data.
questions.relatedConcept: Android App Development - Activity Lifecycle & Configuration Changes
questions.interviewTip: Use ViewModel and SavedStateHandle to retain user input across configuration changes.

questions.question: [Android App Development • Test 1 • Q2] In Jetpack Compose, what triggers Recomposition of a Composable function?
options: Every time an Android system timer ticks (60Hz).
When the device battery percentage changes.
Only when invalidate() is called manually on Canvas.
When a State object read by the composable changes its value.
questions.correctAnswer: When a State object read by the composable changes its value.
questions.explanation: Compose tracks read states. When a State<T> mutates, only the composables that observe that state are intelligently recomposed.
questions.hint: State mutations trigger recomposition of observing composables.
questions.relatedConcept: Android App Development - Jetpack Compose Declarative Recomposition
questions.interviewTip: Use 'remember { mutableStateOf(...) }' to preserve state across recompositions.
